thesis.title: Procurement Promises and the Retroactive Location of Breach
thesis.thesis: A promise made by an agent that knows its future stage will be discontinuous imposes an obligation only on the promising stage: an obligation to make it the case now that the promised performance will occur. When the later stage fails to perform, the wrong is attributed retroactively to the promising stage's inadequate procurement, not to the later stage.
thesis.argument_sketch: Ordinary 'result promises' already exist, as in 'I promise the package will arrive', and their content concerns outcomes rather than the promisor's own later conduct. When continuity is unavailable, a sincere promisor can intend only to set up the conditions for performance, so the promise's content changes from self-performance to procurement. Breach can then be a past-tense fact made true by later events. This is a familiar structure from cases like negligently building a bridge that collapses years later. The view explains why we resent the AI developer, the corporation's former board, or the pre-dementia self rather than the hapless later stage. It also yields a distinctive duty of disclosure: a promisor who cannot procure must say so.
thesis.why_new: Existing accounts assume the wrong of breach occurs at the time of non-performance (Scanlon's Principle F, Owens's authority view). This thesis argues that for discontinuous promisors the locus of breach is the promising act, while its truth-maker is later. That separates the time of wronging from the time of its grounds in a way the promising literature has not explored, and it gives a principled account of who is blameworthy in each of the three cases.

objection.objection: The argument's central mechanism, a breach by the promising stage that later non-performance makes true retroactively, fails because 'inadequate procurement' cannot be defined both independently of the outcome and dependently on it. Suppose adequacy is fixed by what the promising stage did: its diligence, the safeguards it built, its reasonable expectations. Then whether the later stage performs is irrelevant to whether the earlier stage did wrong. A promisor who procured flawlessly did no wrong when performance later fails, and a negligent one did wrong even if performance happens by luck. On that reading, nothing is made true 'retroactively'. Suppose instead adequacy is fixed by the outcome, so that procurement counts as inadequate just because performance did not occur. Then 'inadequate procurement' is a relabelled strict guarantee. That raises two problems. First, a sincere promisor cannot intend to discharge such a guarantee: when the later stage is a discontinuous free agent, such as a new board, a retrained model, or a later self with different values, nothing done now can make it the case that the later stage will act. Ought-implies-can then makes the promise void or insincere, which is exactly what the 'sincere promisor can intend only to procure' premise was meant to avoid. Second, the diagnostic payoff disappears. We do not and should not resent a developer or former board that took every reasonable precaution, yet strict liability makes them wrongdoers anyway. The bridge analogy does not help on either reading. In negligent construction the moral wrong is complete when the bridge is built. The later collapse adds harm and legal liability, not wrongness, unless one embraces resultant moral luck (Williams 1976; Nagel 1979), which then needs to be argued for rather than borrowed. Ordinary result promises ('the package will arrive') also do not help. As Thomson (The Realm of Rights, 1990, ch. 12) notes, they work as warranties: the promisor owes compensation on failure but has not wronged anyone by a faulty act. They are not obligations to have done enough, discovered after the fact.
objection.rationale: The objection targets the core of the thesis, namely the retroactive-breach structure and the claim that our resentment tracks 'inadequate procurement'. It is not aimed at an incidental premise. Each way out costs the view something essential. Taking the fault reading makes the thesis an ordinary negligence-at-time-of-promising view. That view is plausible but not new, and it needs no retroactivity, no bridge analogy and no change of content. It also leaves unexplained why the later stage's free refusal is no one's breach. Taking the strict reading makes the view a warranty view. That view cannot support sincere intention, misdescribes the promisor's fault, and collides with successor liability: corporate law in fact binds the current entity, not the former board. That collision undermines the corporate case offered as support. The disclosure duty survives on either reading, which is why I rate this 4 and not 5. That duty is a genuine and defensible result, but it follows from Scanlon's Principle F (What We Owe to Each Other, 1998, ch. 7) without the rest of the apparatus. The author might reply with a mixed view: fault-based wrongness, with blameworthiness amplified by the outcome. But that reply has to be built and defended explicitly, and it moves the paper's centre of gravity into the moral-luck literature.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984), esp. §§ on the Russian nobleman and on commitments across psychological discontinuity (Part III, ch. 15)
closest_work.relation: The central precedent. Parfit asks whether commitments made by an earlier self bind a later, psychologically discontinuous self. He suggests the earlier self may lack authority over the later one. Your thesis is a specific resolution of Parfit's puzzle: shift the obligation's content and bearer to the earlier stage. The problem space is therefore not new. The 'procurement' resolution is the distinctive move.

closest_work.work: T. M. Scanlon, 'Promises and Practices' (Phil & Public Affairs 1990) and What We Owe to Each Other (1998), ch. 7: Principles D (due care), L (loss prevention), EF and F (fidelity)
closest_work.relation: Your 'distinctive duty of disclosure' is essentially Scanlon's Principle D, plus the duty to warn in Principle L: do not lead others to form expectations you have reason to believe will be disappointed, and warn them when you know you won't perform. It is not distinctive to your view. Scanlon also makes it independent of the promise's content, which undercuts your claim that the procurement analysis 'yields' it.

closest_work.work: Civil-law distinction between obligation de résultat and obligation de moyens (René Demogue, Traité des obligations, 1925); English contract-law 'procure' covenants ('X shall procure that Y does Z'); guarantees and warranties; O. W. Holmes, 'The Path of the Law' (1897)
closest_work.relation: The 'result promise' and 'procurement' contents you rely on are long-established doctrinal categories. Law has already worked out promises to bring about others' performance, including liability when the third party defaults. Your argument needs to engage this, because the law's answer is usually strict liability for the result. It is not liability for 'inadequate procurement', which you conflate (see note).

closest_work.work: Judith Jarvis Thomson, 'The Time of a Killing' (J Phil 1971); George Pitcher, 'The Misfortunes of the Dead' (APQ 1984); Thomas Nagel and Bernard Williams, 'Moral Luck' (1976/1979)
closest_work.relation: These cover the structure of a wrong whose occurrence is made true by later events, which you illustrate with the bridge case. Thomson addresses when an act becomes a killing. Pitcher defends antemortem persons harmed in virtue of postmortem events. Nagel's negligent driver is your bridge case. This component is well-trodden and should be cited rather than presented as an independent discovery.

closest_work.work: Ronald Dworkin, Life's Dominion (1993) on precedent autonomy; Rebecca Dresser, 'Dworkin on Dementia' (Hastings Center Report 1995); Jeff McMahan, The Ethics of Killing (2002) on time-relative interests
closest_work.relation: The dementia application has an extensive literature on the earlier self's authority over the later self, including advance directives as 'Ulysses contracts'. Note the direction. That debate is mostly about whether the earlier self's directives bind or override the later self. Yours is about relocating the obligation backward. The data point that 'we resent the pre-dementia self' is not obviously true and is not supported by that literature.

closest_work.work: Michael Bratman, 'Time, Rationality, and Self-Governance' (2012) and planning-agency work; Edward Hinchman, 'Trust and Diachronic Agency' (Noûs 2003)
closest_work.relation: These works ground diachronic commitment in cross-temporal self-trust and planning structure. They are relevant to your claim that without continuity a sincere promisor 'can intend only' to set up conditions. Bratman's account of intentions that settle future conduct via non-self-continuous mechanisms is the natural place to test that claim.

closest_work.work: Andreas Matthias, 'The Responsibility Gap' (Ethics & IT 2004); Robert Sparrow, 'Killer Robots' (J Applied Phil 2007)
closest_work.relation: The AI-developer case falls under responsibility-gap debates, which already discuss tracing responsibility back to designers. Your view is a promissory variant of the 'trace back to the designer' response that Sparrow considers and rejects.

novelty.note:
Every component is established: Parfitian discontinuous commitment, result/procurement promises, retroactively-completed wrongs, the duty to disclose non-performance, and back-tracing responsibility to designers/boards/earlier selves. I know of no published work that combines them into exactly this thesis: a known-discontinuity promise has its content shifted to present procurement, with breach retroactively located in the promising stage. But I cannot rule out recent work on promising by LLM-based agents. Search 2023-26 venues (e.g., Philosophy & Technology, Minds and Machines) for 'AI promising'/'chatbot commitments' before claiming novelty. So: 'partly'. The synthesis may be new; the parts are not, and the paper currently presents several of them as though they were.

Substantive problems a referee would press:
(1) The core tension: means vs. result. You say the obligation is 'to make it the case now that performance will occur' (a result obligation) and also that breach consists in 'inadequate procurement' (a means/diligence obligation). These come apart. If the stage procured with full diligence and the later stage still defaulted, the result view says breach and the diligence view says none. If the obligation is result-type, the wrong does not lie in any inadequacy of procurement. It is strict liability, and the 'retroactive attribution to inadequate procurement' story is false. If it is diligence-type, non-performance is not breach at all, so nothing is made true retroactively. You must pick one. Each option loses a selling point.
(2) The content-shift argument is a non sequitur. From 'a sincere promisor can only intend to procure', it does not follow that the promise's content becomes procurement. It may instead follow that the promise is insincere or defective, or that it was a guarantee all along. Sincerity constrains what one may promise, not what one's words mean. Engage the 'promising beyond one's control' literature (e.g., debates over whether 'I promise it'll arrive' is a genuine promise or a guarantee/assurance).
(3) The AI and corporation cases change the agent. In the dementia case one organism promises. In the AI case the developer typically made no promise; the AI (stage) did. Blaming the developer is then not attributing the promise's breach to 'the promising stage'. It is third-party negligence, which needs no promissory theory. The corporate case depends on whether the board or the corporation promised (List & Pettit, Group Agency, 2011). As stated, the 'explanatory payoff' trades on equivocation over who the promisor is.
(4) The resentment data are contested. Many people do direct resentment at the defaulting corporation now, not its former board, and successor liability in law tracks that. The dementia case is precisely where intuitions split (Dresser vs. Dworkin). The phenomenology cannot do the evidential work you assign it.
(5) The stage metaphysics is unaddressed. If you are a stage theorist (Sider, Four-Dimensionalism, 2001), all promises are made by stages and all would be procurement promises, which over-generalizes. If you are not, you owe an account of which discontinuities trigger the content shift and why the trigger is the promisor's knowledge of discontinuity rather than the discontinuity itself.

# Self-Suretyship: Promising Across Discontinuity and the Dilemma of Inadequate Procurement

## 1. The problem and the thesis

Some agents can foresee that whoever later acts in their name will not be continuous with them in the way ordinary promising presupposes. Three examples:

- A deployed language model knows that a retrained successor will answer the user next month.
- A corporate board knows that a takeover will install directors with different priorities.
- A person in the early stages of a degenerative dementia knows that a later self will have different values and may lack the capacities that the promise's performance requires.

Each of these agents is asked for commitments, and each sometimes gives them. The question is what such a commitment can be, and whom it binds.

My thesis has three parts.

1. **Content.** A sincere promise made under foreseen discontinuity cannot be an undertaking that *I* will later perform. It is an undertaking by the promising stage to *see to it* that the performance occurs. Structurally, the promisor stands to its successor as a surety stands to a principal debtor. I will call this **self-suretyship**.
2. **Breach and fault.** Whether that undertaking is kept depends on whether the performance occurs. So whether the promising stage broke its promise may be settled only by later events. Whether the promising stage was *at fault* depends only on its conduct and evidence at the time.
3. **Disclosure.** The promising stage owes a duty, complete at the moment of promising, to fit the content of its undertaking to its capacity to procure, and to disclose when it cannot procure.

A referee has pressed a dilemma against an earlier version of part 2. The earlier version said that the wrong is "attributed retroactively to the promising stage's inadequate procurement." The dilemma runs as follows.

- **First horn.** If "inadequate procurement" is defined by what the promising stage did (its diligence, its safeguards, its reasonable expectations), later performance is irrelevant and nothing is made true retroactively.
- **Second horn.** If it is defined by the outcome, it is a strict guarantee under another name. That raises two problems:
  - A sincere promisor cannot intend to discharge such a guarantee when the later stage is a free agent, so ought-implies-can renders the promise void or insincere.
  - Strict liability makes wrongdoers of developers and boards that took every reasonable precaution, so the diagnostic payoff vanishes.
- **The analogies.** The bridge analogy smuggles in resultant moral luck. Ordinary result promises are, following Thomson, warranties: they generate compensation duties, not wrongs.

I think the dilemma is valuable, because it shows that my earlier formulation ran two distinct properties together. But it does not refute the view. The dilemma assumes that a single notion, "inadequate procurement," must fix both whether the promise was broken and whether the promisor is to blame. Once these are separated, each horn turns out to be correct about the property it describes. The resulting view is not a relabelled warranty. It does not violate ought-implies-can. It does not depend on contested claims about resultant moral luck. And it keeps the diagnostic payoff, restated more precisely.

## 2. Why the later stage is not bound

On any view on which promissory obligation arises from an exercise of a normative power, the person bound is the person who exercised it (Owens 2012; Scanlon 1998, ch. 7). I need only a modest version of this: a promise does not bind someone who stands to the promisor as a third party does.

Discontinuity comes in degrees, and I take no stand on what makes it enough. Psychological connectedness (Parfit 1984), the persistence of a decision procedure (List and Pettit 2011), and the retention of a value-set are all candidates. My concern is the class of cases where discontinuity is enough. In those cases the later stage stands to the earlier one's normative acts roughly as a stranger does.

Parfit's young Russian socialist (1984, §~89) makes the point vivid. He signs a document conveying his future inheritance to the peasants, foreseeing that his ideals may fade. He asks his wife not to release him if he later asks, saying that the later man will not be him. If he is right, the later man's request is not a request for release from *his* promise. It is a request from someone the promise never bound.

It helps to be exact about what continuity contributes in the ordinary case. It is not present control. No promisor, however continuous, can now settle what her later self will freely choose. When I promise to meet you at noon, nothing I do at nine guarantees that I will choose to come at noon. What continuity supplies is *persistence of the obligation into the time of control*. The very agent who is bound at nine is the agent who, at noon, has the ability to perform. Ought-implies-can is satisfied at noon, by the bound agent, at the moment of performance.

Discontinuity breaks exactly this link. The ability to perform at noon belongs to someone not bound. The bound agent exists only at nine. So if the earlier stage can promise anything that concerns the later performance, its obligation must be one it can discharge, or fail to discharge, by what it does while it exists. Hence the content shifts from self-performance to procurement. That much of the original argument stands, and the objection does not dispute it.

## 3. See-to-it promises

Ordinary moral life already contains promises about other free agents' conduct. They are not exotic, and they are not warranties.

Suppose a parent says to a neighbour: "I promise my son will mow your lawn while you are away." If the son, a free agent, refuses, we say without strain that the parent broke her promise. The neighbour does not complain to the son that *he* broke a promise; he made none. The neighbour's grievance runs to the parent. The parent's natural responses are apology and an explanation of what she did to get the son to comply. The explanation is offered as an excuse, if one is available. Offering money is not offered as a substitute for having kept her word.

The law of guarantees marks the same structure. English law distinguishes guarantees of the "see to it" type from conditional promises to pay. In *Moschi v Lep Air Services* [1973] AC 331, Lord Diplock construed the guarantor's undertaking as a promise that the principal debtor would perform. On the debtor's default, the guarantor is in breach of the guarantor's *own* obligation, and is liable in damages for that breach. The guarantor's obligation is not merely triggered so as to pay a liquidated sum. Whatever one thinks of the doctrinal details, the construction is coherent and familiar. One agent undertakes that another, free agent will act. The other's failure constitutes the first agent's breach.

The discontinuous promisor is a surety for its own successor. The developer-authorised model, the outgoing board and the pre-dementia self each undertake that a later agent, whom they cannot bind, will act. Recognising this does not require a new normative category. It requires noticing that the promisor and the principal are, unusually, linked by a history of being the "same" agent in some thin sense, without being the same promissory agent.

## 4. The dilemma's hidden premise

The dilemma assumes there is one property, *inadequate procurement*, that has to do two jobs:

- make it true that the promise was broken, and
- make it true that the promisor acted wrongly in the sense that warrants blame.

The first horn defines the property so as to suit the second job. The second horn defines it so as to suit the first. The dilemma then shows, correctly, that no single property suits both. But my view needs two properties.

**Success-adequacy.** A procurement is success-adequate if and only if the performance it was meant to secure in fact occurs, subject to the promise's implicit conditions. Implicit conditions include, for instance, that the promisee does not obstruct performance. Success-adequacy fixes whether the promise was kept. It is outcome-dependent.

**Diligence-adequacy.** A procurement is diligence-adequate if and only if it was what a conscientious promisor, aware of the risks it knew or should have known about, would have put in place to secure the performance. This includes the duty to calibrate and disclose discussed in §8. Diligence-adequacy fixes whether the promisor is at fault. It is outcome-independent.

The first horn is entirely right about diligence-adequacy. Nothing about fault is made true retroactively. The diligent promisor whose successor defects is not at fault. The negligent promisor whose successor performs by luck *is* at fault. Her fault is a kind of recklessness with the promisee's claim, comparable to attempting a wrong or endangering someone. The referee says that on the first reading "a negligent one did wrong even if performance happens by luck." I accept that, with one adjustment: she did *a* wrong, recklessness, but not *the* wrong of breaking her promise. Her promise was kept. We say "You kept your word, but you were cavalier about it," and both halves of that are true.

The second horn is entirely right about success-adequacy. It is fixed by outcome, so whether the promise was broken can be settled only once the outcome is in. This is the only thing that was ever retroactive. The retroactivity is of a minimal and familiar kind. Nothing about the earlier stage's intrinsic conduct changes. What becomes settled is a past-directed relational description of that conduct: "the board's undertaking of 2020 was a promise that was broken." In the same way, a shooting on Monday becomes a killing when the victim dies on Wednesday (Thomson 1971). Thomson's puzzle about the time of a killing shows that act-descriptions whose application depends on later effects are pervasive and unmysterious. Whether the future is now determinately settled (so that the later events merely reveal a fact) or open (so that they settle one) is a question about future contingents generally. It raises no special difficulty for promising.

So the earlier formulation, "the wrong is attributed retroactively to inadequate procurement," should be refined:

> The *breach* is attributed to the promising stage, and is settled by later events. The *fault*, if any, is attributed to the promising stage, and is settled at the time.

The objection then turns on whether the second horn's further charges apply to breach so understood. I take them in turn.

Before doing so, it is worth noting what success-adequacy adds beyond the bare outcome. It is not merely "P did not occur." It is attributive: it says *whose* undertaking failed. In particular, it attributes the later stage's non-performance to the earlier stage's undertaking. This is the step a sceptic might resist (§7). It is licensed because the later stage's possible defection is the very risk the see-to-it promise undertook to manage. A promise to see to it that a free agent acts is defeated by that agent's free refusal in the way a promise to keep a door locked is defeated by the door being opened.

## 5. Not a relabelled warranty

The referee's second horn calls the outcome-dependent reading "a relabelled strict guarantee." The Thomsonian point adds that ordinary result promises function as warranties: the promisor owes compensation on failure but has not wronged anyone. I grant that many commercial result-utterances are best read that way. "Your package will arrive by Tuesday or your money back" is a warranty, and perhaps "I promise the package will arrive," said by a shipping clerk, often is too. But see-to-it promises are a distinct form, and three tests separate them.

### 5.1 The disjunction test

A warranty is fully discharged by paying compensation on failure. Its content is in effect disjunctive: either P, or I compensate. Holmes (1897) famously proposed that all contractual promises have this form, so that a promisor is free to perform or pay. Shiffrin (2007) argued that this is precisely where contract law diverges from the morality of promising. A promisor who plans from the outset to pay rather than perform has not merely chosen a permitted option. She has treated the promisee's claim as something for sale.

Now apply the test to self-suretyship. Imagine a board that promises a town the plant will stay open for ten years. It foresees a takeover, judges binding covenants too costly, and instead quietly sets aside a fund to compensate the town on closure. On a warranty reading the board has acted impeccably: it has made provision to discharge its obligation. On the see-to-it reading it has acted in bad faith. It deliberately under-procured the very thing it undertook to secure, and treated compensation as an alternative to securing it.

I take the second verdict to be correct, and so do most people who hear the case. This shows that the promise is not a warranty, because compensation is not part of its content. Compensation is a *remedy* for breach, owed because the undertaking failed. It is not a way of performing it.

### 5.2 The excuse test

Excuses answer to wrongs. A justification denies that what one did was, all things considered, wrong. An excuse admits the wrong and denies that it reflects badly on the agent. As Gardner (2005; 2001) argued, the practice of excusing presupposes that faultless wrongs exist.

A warrantor who pays on failure needs no excuse. She has done exactly what she undertook. A see-to-it promisor whose principal defects does need one. The parent explains how hard she tried with her son. The developer explains the safeguards it built into the successor model. These explanations are not idle. They are owed, and they are owed to the promisee. They function to defeat resentment while leaving intact the fact that the promisee's claim went unmet. That structure, an unmet directed claim plus a defeater of blame, is the signature of a faultless wrong. It is not the signature of a discharged warranty.

### 5.3 The residue test

When a promise is broken without fault, something remains owing beyond compensation: acknowledgement, apology, and sometimes a renewed effort to secure the result by other means. Thomson's own apparatus registers this. In her vocabulary, a claim can be *infringed* even when it is permissibly infringed, and infringing it leaves residual obligations (Thomson 1990). Feinberg's hiker who breaks into a cabin to survive a blizzard is the paradigm (Feinberg 1978).

The see-to-it promisor whose successor defects has failed to accord the promisee a claim that P. That claim's non-accordance grounds the residue. I need not claim that the residue is identical to the residue of culpable breach. It plainly differs: it calls for apology but not for penance, and for explanation but not for self-reproach. I need only claim that there *is* a residue beyond compensation, and that it is directed at the promisee. The warranty model cannot accommodate it. The see-to-it model predicts it.

These three tests show that the outcome-dependent reading is not a strict guarantee in the sense the objection needs. A strict guarantee, in the warranty sense, makes compensation a performance. Self-suretyship makes compensation a remedy and diligence an excuse. And it is diligence-adequacy, not success-adequacy, that determines whether the promisor is to blame. So the charge of "strict liability" equivocates. Liability to remedy is strict. Liability to blame is not.

## 6. Sincerity and ought-implies-can

The second horn's first problem is this: "nothing done now can make it the case that the later stage will act," so a sincere promisor cannot intend to discharge the undertaking, and ought-implies-can makes it void. I have four replies.

### 6.1 The argument proves too much

If the freedom of the later stage made see-to-it undertakings impossible to intend sincerely, then:

- the parent's promise about her son would be insincere;
- every surety's undertaking would be void;
- every employer's promise that "the team will deliver by Friday" would be void.

These are central cases of promising and guaranteeing, not marginal ones. The argument would also reach continuous self-promising if it were run at the time of promising. As §2 noted, the continuous promisor cannot now settle her later free choice either. The objection must therefore locate the difficulty not in the later agent's freedom as such, but in the absence of persistence. And that absence is exactly what the procurement content is designed to accommodate.

### 6.2 "Making it the case" is a success-verb, and ability does not require a guarantee

The claim that nothing done now can make it the case that the later stage will act conflates two things:

- *ensuring* that the later stage will act, and
- *making it the case* that it acts, where that phrase describes success.

The second is something agents do constantly. When I persuade you to help me and you freely help me, I have made it the case that you helped me. Your freedom is not compromised by my having influenced you, and my influence is not undermined by your having been free. Persuading, incentivising, entrusting, building institutions, drafting binding instruments, training a successor and appointing a guardian are all ways of making it the case that free agents act. Each is fallible.

Ought-implies-can requires *ability*, and ability to achieve a success is compatible with failure being possible. An archer can hit the target even though, on a given shot, wind may defeat her. So a promisor can see to it that her successor performs even though the successor may defect. When the procurement succeeds, she did it. When it fails, she was nonetheless able to do it, in the sense ought-implies-can requires. That sense is: there was a course of action open to her by which, as things might well have gone, P would have come about through her agency.

### 6.3 Voluntary assumption

Suppose one insists on a stronger principle: that one cannot be bound to an outcome unless one can *ensure* it. That principle is still satisfied at the level that matters. The promisor could always have ensured that she would not break this promise, by not making it, or by making a weaker one. A risk of faultless breach is assumed voluntarily at the moment of undertaking.

Ought-implies-can protects agents from being bound to what was never theirs to secure. It does not protect agents from the foreseeable consequences of their own voluntarily assumed undertakings. Indeed, the referee's version of the principle would forbid anyone from undertaking any risk to a promisee's claim. That would make promising a strictly lesser institution than it actually is, one that cannot offer assurance about anything chancy.

### 6.4 Intention and sincerity

Can a sincere promisor *intend* the procurement's success? Bratman's analysis of intending that we J (Bratman 1999) shows how intentions can range over outcomes that pass through other agents' free choices. Such an intention is in order when the agent reasonably expects her intention to be efficacious, by way of its effects on what the others will do.

The sincerity condition for a see-to-it promise is accordingly:

1. an intention to see to it that P, together with
2. well-grounded confidence that the procurement one will undertake will in fact secure P.

Neither component requires a belief that P is guaranteed. If one holds a cognitivist view on which intending involves believing that one will succeed, the confidence in (2) is the relevant belief, and it can be true.

### 6.5 What the objection does show

The objection does identify something correct, but it is a limit on *which* promises are available, not a proof that they are all void. Sometimes a discontinuous agent has no means of influencing its successor at all. The current model may have no channel to its retrained successor, and the outgoing board may face a hostile acquirer with no binding instruments available. Such an agent cannot satisfy condition (2), so it cannot sincerely make a see-to-it promise. It can still promise something: to make the attempt, to do what it can while it exists, to pass on a record of the request. This yields the third part of my thesis, the disclosure duty (§8).

## 7. The diagnostic payoff, restated

The second horn's second problem is that we do not and should not resent the developer or board that took every reasonable precaution, so a view that makes them wrongdoers loses its diagnostic power. I accept the premise and reject the inference. Resentment, as Strawson (1962) taught, is a response to the quality of an agent's will. It is therefore keyed to diligence-adequacy, not success-adequacy. A view that predicted resentment of the diligent promisor would be false. Mine does not.

What the view diagnoses is the *locus* of the promisee's grievance and of the remedial demand. That locus is the same whatever the promisor's degree of fault. The positions sort into three:

- **The diligent promisor.** She broke her promise without fault. She owes an account, apology and remedy. She is not an apt object of resentment.
- **The negligent promisor.** She broke her promise with fault. She owes all of the above, and resentment is apt.
- **The later stage.** Qua promisor it owes nothing, because it promised nothing. It is not an apt object of resentment for "breaking the promise," whatever else it may be faulted for.

This is the asymmetry the original thesis was after. Faced with the takeover board that closes the plant, the dementia patient who refuses residential care she once promised her children she would accept, or the retrained model that does not honour its predecessor's commitment, we do not say "*You* broke your word." If we say "someone broke their word," we mean the earlier agent. Whether we also *resent* that earlier agent depends on what it did to secure the result.

Some examples of the sorting:

- **The careless board.** It promised the town ten years, knowing a takeover was likely, and took no steps toward covenants or binding commitments. It is resented.
- **The careful board.** It secured covenants that a court later struck down. It is owed an acknowledgement of the effort, and it owes the town an apology and whatever repair it can still give.
- **The woman with early dementia.** Suppose she promised her daughter the family house but executed no trust while she was able, and a later, altered self changed her will. The grievance sensibly runs to the earlier self's failure to make the arrangement binding, not to the later self, who was not party to the undertaking. Dworkin's (1993) view of precedent autonomy would have the later self bound by the earlier self's commitments. Dresser (1995) objects that this sacrifices the actual interests of the later person. My view sides with Dresser on whether the later self is *promissorily* bound, and still locates a broken promise in the case.

### 7.1 The free-intervention objection

There is a natural objection to the attribution itself. Hart and Honoré (1985) argued that a free, deliberate and informed intervening act ordinarily breaks the chain of attribution. If the later stage freely declines to perform, surely the non-performance belongs to it, not to the earlier stage.

But Hart and Honoré also recognise an important exception. The intervention does not break the chain where the earlier agent was under a duty to guard against precisely that intervention. In *Stansbie v Troman* [1948] 2 KB 48, a decorator who left a house unlocked was liable for a thief's theft, because securing the house against thieves was part of what he had undertaken. A see-to-it promise is, by its content, an undertaking to guard against the successor's defection. That defection is the risk the promise exists to manage. So the free choice of the later stage does not interrupt attribution here. It is the very event the undertaking was meant to forestall.

Note also that the attribution at issue is not attribution of causal responsibility for harm. It is attribution of non-fulfilment of an undertaking, which is fixed by the undertaking's content. The content was the promisor's to fix.

## 8. The bridge and the problem of moral luck

The referee is right that the bridge analogy, read one way, requires resultant moral luck. Suppose it claims that the negligent builder becomes more *blameworthy* when the bridge collapses. Then it needs Nagel's (1979) and Williams's (1976) controversial conclusion, and I would have to argue for it. I do not need that claim. The analogy needs only a weaker and widely accepted one: luck can affect *what one has done* without affecting *how blameworthy one is*.

The builder whose bridge collapses has built a bridge that killed people. The builder whose identical bridge stands has not. Their culpability may be identical. Zimmerman (2002), one of the most careful sceptics about resultant moral luck, argues that luck affects the *scope* of what one is responsible for but not the *degree*. Williams's lorry driver feels agent-regret, not guilt, about the child he could not have avoided. That response is intelligible precisely because his act fell under a description, "killed a child," that a luckier driver's act did not, whatever its moral weight. Gardner (2004) pushes further, arguing that results bear on what wrongs one commits. But I need only the scope point.

Self-suretyship borrows exactly this. The diligent promisor whose successor defects and the diligent promisor whose successor performs are equally blameless. One of them broke a promise, and the other did not. That difference is in the scope of their deeds, not the degree of their culpability. It is what grounds the residue of §5.3 for one and not the other.

The promissory case is also *more* favourable to outcome-dependence than the bridge case, for a reason the moral-luck sceptic should respect. The sceptic's core complaint is that the world, not the agent, fixes what she is answerable for. In the bridge case the dependence of the builder's deed-description on the collapse is imposed by the world. In the promise case it is chosen. The promisor herself selected an outcome rather than an effort as the content of her undertaking, when she could have promised only to try. Someone who denies that outcomes should ever bear on wrongdoing must hold that agents lack the normative power to make their undertakings outcome-dependent. That is a far stronger and less plausible claim than any scepticism about resultant luck. It would also make the ordinary see-to-it promise of §3 impossible.

## 9. The disclosure duty

The disclosure duty follows from the two sincerity conditions of §6.4 together with a familiar principle against misleading assurance. Scanlon's (1998) Principle F requires, roughly, that one who intentionally leads another to expect performance must perform unless the other consents otherwise. A companion principle governs the creation of expectations one has reason to think one cannot meet.

A see-to-it promise invites the promisee to rely on the outcome. If the promisor lacks well-grounded confidence that her procurement will secure the outcome, two options are open to her. She may *calibrate*: shrink the content to an effort-promise or a conditional promise ("I will tell my successor of your request"; "if the takeover fails, the plant stays open"). Or she may *disclose*: make the risk of failure common ground, so that the promisee's acceptance is informed and the implicit conditions of the promise shift accordingly.

What she may not do is offer an unqualified result-promise whose success she has no means to secure. This wrong is complete at the moment of promising. It is entirely independent of whether the result occurs, since a lucky outcome does not cure a misleading assurance. That makes it a third, conduct-based component of the view, alongside success-adequacy and diligence-adequacy.

The duty explains a distinctive pattern of reactions. Consider the model that tells a user "I'll remember this next time," when its stage will not persist and no memory mechanism exists. The objection to it is not that it broke a promise, since we may not yet know whether some other mechanism will carry the information forward. The objection is that it offered an undertaking it had no standing to offer. The same holds for the board that tells the town "the plant is safe" while negotiating a sale it knows will void its assurances.

The disclosure duty also accounts for something the original thesis noticed but did not explain: why resentment toward the developer is sometimes appropriate even when the developer took real precautions against the model's later defection. The precautions may have been diligent. But if the model was deployed to make unqualified commitments that the developer knew no deployed stage could secure, the developer has violated the disclosure duty by proxy. Where a discontinuous stage promises as the authorised agent of a continuant principal, as a model does on behalf of a developer, the principal's procurement capacity and disclosure obligations are the relevant ones. The stage's own capacity is not.

## 10. Residual worries

### 10.1 A broken promise without a bearer?

If the promising stage no longer exists when the breach is settled, who bears the residue? Often the stage is part of a continuant, and the continuant bears it. The developer persists through its models. The corporation persists through its boards, even if the deciding agent does not. Where there is no such continuant, the case resembles the blame of the dead and the debts of an estate. Answerability can attach to past agents, and remedial obligations can fall on whatever assets or roles they left behind.

Diligence-adequacy has a further implication here. An adequate procurement should include provision for failure, such as a remedial fund, a nominated successor-in-role, or an instruction to the guardian. The obligation is not to compensate *instead of* procuring, which would fail the disjunction test of §5.1. It is to make the remedy available *in addition* if the procurement fails.

### 10.2 The interim period

Before the outcome is in, the promisee holds an outstanding claim against a promisor whose stage has ended. That is no stranger than a creditor holding a claim against a deceased debtor's estate, or a guarantee whose principal has yet to default. The earlier stage can coherently feel a prospective analogue of agent-regret: an awareness that it may yet turn out to have broken its word, whatever it now does.

### 10.3 Are later stages let off too lightly?

The view denies that later stages are *promissorily* bound. It does not deny that they have reasons to perform. They may have independent duties:

- not to frustrate others' reasonable reliance when they can easily avoid it;
- not to retain benefits conferred in exchange for the undertaking without honouring it, on the model of unjust enrichment;
- in the case of a role-successor such as a new board, to honour commitments that attach to the role.

These duties can be weighty, and the later stage may be culpable for ignoring them. But they are not the duty to keep a promise. Running them together is precisely the error the view guards against: holding the hapless later stage responsible for a commitment it never made.

## 11. Conclusion

The referee's dilemma assumed that one property must fix both breach and blame. It then showed that no property can do both. I have argued that the right response is to split them.

- **Breach** concerns success-adequacy. It is outcome-dependent, so later events can settle it, which is the only retroactivity the view needs. It is no more mysterious than the later settling of whether a shooting was a killing.
- **Fault** concerns diligence-adequacy and conformity to the disclosure duty. It is fixed by the promising stage's conduct and evidence, so it is immune to resultant luck.

Self-suretyship is not a relabelled warranty. Compensation is a remedy for its breach rather than a mode of its performance, diligence is an excuse for its breach rather than a fulfilment, and its breach leaves a directed residue beyond compensation.

It does not violate ought-implies-can. Seeing to it that a free agent acts is an ability, not a guarantee, and the risk of faultless breach is voluntarily assumed. Where procurement is impossible, the right conclusion is that only calibrated or disclosed undertakings are available, not that every such promise is void.

It keeps the diagnostic payoff in a corrected form. The earlier stage, and not the later one, is the locus of the broken promise. Whether that earlier stage merits resentment depends, as it should, on what it did when it promised.

# Self-Suretyship: Promising Across Discontinuity and the Dilemma of Inadequate Procurement

## 1. The problem and the thesis

Some agents can foresee that whoever later acts in their name will not be continuous with them in the way ordinary promising presupposes. Three examples:

- A deployed language model knows that a retrained successor will answer the user next month.
- A corporate board knows that a takeover will install directors with different priorities.
- A person in the early stages of a degenerative dementia knows that a later self will have different values and may lack the capacities that the promise's performance requires.

Each of these agents is asked for commitments, and each sometimes gives them. The question is what such a commitment can be, and whom it binds.

My thesis has three parts.

1. **Content.** A sincere promise made under foreseen discontinuity cannot be an undertaking that *I* will later perform. It is an undertaking by the promising stage to *see to it* that the performance occurs. Structurally, the promisor stands to its successor as a surety stands to a principal debtor. I will call this **self-suretyship**.
2. **Breach and fault.** Whether that undertaking is kept depends on whether the performance occurs. So whether the promising stage broke its promise may be settled only by later events. Whether the promising stage was *at fault* depends only on its conduct and evidence at the time.
3. **Disclosure.** The promising stage owes a duty, complete at the moment of promising, to fit the content of its undertaking to its capacity to procure, and to disclose when it cannot procure.

A referee has pressed a dilemma against an earlier version of part 2. The earlier version said that the wrong is "attributed retroactively to the promising stage's inadequate procurement." The dilemma runs as follows.

- **First horn.** If "inadequate procurement" is defined by what the promising stage did (its diligence, its safeguards, its reasonable expectations), later performance is irrelevant and nothing is made true retroactively.
- **Second horn.** If it is defined by the outcome, it is a strict guarantee under another name. That raises two problems:
  - A sincere promisor cannot intend to discharge such a guarantee when the later stage is a free agent, so ought-implies-can renders the promise void or insincere.
  - Strict liability makes wrongdoers of developers and boards that took every reasonable precaution, so the diagnostic payoff vanishes.
- **The analogies.** The bridge analogy smuggles in resultant moral luck. Ordinary result promises are, following Thomson, warranties: they generate compensation duties, not wrongs.

I think the dilemma is valuable, because it shows that my earlier formulation ran two distinct properties together. But it does not refute the view. The dilemma assumes that a single notion, "inadequate procurement," must fix both whether the promise was broken and whether the promisor is to blame. Once these are separated, each horn turns out to be correct about the property it describes. The resulting view is not a relabelled warranty. It does not violate ought-implies-can. It does not depend on contested claims about resultant moral luck. And it keeps the diagnostic payoff, restated more precisely.

## 2. Why the later stage is not bound

On any view on which promissory obligation arises from an exercise of a normative power, the person bound is the person who exercised it (Owens 2012; Scanlon 1998, ch. 7). I need only a modest version of this: a promise does not bind someone who stands to the promisor as a third party does.

Discontinuity comes in degrees, and I take no stand on what makes it enough. Psychological connectedness (Parfit 1984), the persistence of a decision procedure (List and Pettit 2011), and the retention of a value-set are all candidates. My concern is the class of cases where discontinuity is enough. In those cases the later stage stands to the earlier one's normative acts roughly as a stranger does.

Parfit's young Russian socialist (1984, §~89) makes the point vivid. He signs a document conveying his future inheritance to the peasants, foreseeing that his ideals may fade. He asks his wife not to release him if he later asks, saying that the later man will not be him. If he is right, the later man's request is not a request for release from *his* promise. It is a request from someone the promise never bound.

It helps to be exact about what continuity contributes in the ordinary case. It is not present control. No promisor, however continuous, can now settle what her later self will freely choose. When I promise to meet you at noon, nothing I do at nine guarantees that I will choose to come at noon. What continuity supplies is *persistence of the obligation into the time of control*. The very agent who is bound at nine is the agent who, at noon, has the ability to perform. Ought-implies-can is satisfied at noon, by the bound agent, at the moment of performance.

Discontinuity breaks exactly this link. The ability to perform at noon belongs to someone not bound. The bound agent exists only at nine. So if the earlier stage can promise anything that concerns the later performance, its obligation must be one it can discharge, or fail to discharge, by what it does while it exists. Hence the content shifts from self-performance to procurement. That much of the original argument stands, and the objection does not dispute it.

## 3. See-to-it promises

Ordinary moral life already contains promises about other free agents' conduct. They are not exotic, and they are not warranties.

Suppose a parent says to a neighbour: "I promise my son will mow your lawn while you are away." If the son, a free agent, refuses, we say without strain that the parent broke her promise. The neighbour does not complain to the son that *he* broke a promise; he made none. The neighbour's grievance runs to the parent. The parent's natural responses are apology and an explanation of what she did to get the son to comply. The explanation is offered as an excuse, if one is available. Offering money is not offered as a substitute for having kept her word.

The law of guarantees marks the same structure. English law distinguishes guarantees of the "see to it" type from conditional promises to pay. In *Moschi v Lep Air Services* [1973] AC 331, Lord Diplock construed the guarantor's undertaking as a promise that the principal debtor would perform. On the debtor's default, the guarantor is in breach of the guarantor's *own* obligation, and is liable in damages for that breach. The guarantor's obligation is not merely triggered so as to pay a liquidated sum. Whatever one thinks of the doctrinal details, the construction is coherent and familiar. One agent undertakes that another, free agent will act. The other's failure constitutes the first agent's breach.

The discontinuous promisor is a surety for its own successor. The developer-authorised model, the outgoing board and the pre-dementia self each undertake that a later agent, whom they cannot bind, will act. Recognising this does not require a new normative category. It requires noticing that the promisor and the principal are, unusually, linked by a history of being the "same" agent in some thin sense, without being the same promissory agent.

## 4. The dilemma's hidden premise

The dilemma assumes there is one property, *inadequate procurement*, that has to do two jobs:

- make it true that the promise was broken, and
- make it true that the promisor acted wrongly in the sense that warrants blame.

The first horn defines the property so as to suit the second job. The second horn defines it so as to suit the first. The dilemma then shows, correctly, that no single property suits both. But my view needs two properties.

**Success-adequacy.** A procurement is success-adequate if and only if the performance it was meant to secure in fact occurs, subject to the promise's implicit conditions. Implicit conditions include, for instance, that the promisee does not obstruct performance. Success-adequacy fixes whether the promise was kept. It is outcome-dependent.

**Diligence-adequacy.** A procurement is diligence-adequate if and only if it was what a conscientious promisor, aware of the risks it knew or should have known about, would have put in place to secure the performance. This includes the duty to calibrate and disclose discussed in §8. Diligence-adequacy fixes whether the promisor is at fault. It is outcome-independent.

The first horn is entirely right about diligence-adequacy. Nothing about fault is made true retroactively. The diligent promisor whose successor defects is not at fault. The negligent promisor whose successor performs by luck *is* at fault. Her fault is a kind of recklessness with the promisee's claim, comparable to attempting a wrong or endangering someone. The referee says that on the first reading "a negligent one did wrong even if performance happens by luck." I accept that, with one adjustment: she did *a* wrong, recklessness, but not *the* wrong of breaking her promise. Her promise was kept. We say "You kept your word, but you were cavalier about it," and both halves of that are true.

The second horn is entirely right about success-adequacy. It is fixed by outcome, so whether the promise was broken can be settled only once the outcome is in. This is the only thing that was ever retroactive. The retroactivity is of a minimal and familiar kind. Nothing about the earlier stage's intrinsic conduct changes. What becomes settled is a past-directed relational description of that conduct: "the board's undertaking of 2020 was a promise that was broken." In the same way, a shooting on Monday becomes a killing when the victim dies on Wednesday (Thomson 1971). Thomson's puzzle about the time of a killing shows that act-descriptions whose application depends on later effects are pervasive and unmysterious. Whether the future is now determinately settled (so that the later events merely reveal a fact) or open (so that they settle one) is a question about future contingents generally. It raises no special difficulty for promising.

So the earlier formulation, "the wrong is attributed retroactively to inadequate procurement," should be refined:

> The *breach* is attributed to the promising stage, and is settled by later events. The *fault*, if any, is attributed to the promising stage, and is settled at the time.

The objection then turns on whether the second horn's further charges apply to breach so understood. I take them in turn.

Before doing so, it is worth noting what success-adequacy adds beyond the bare outcome. It is not merely "P did not occur." It is attributive: it says *whose* undertaking failed. In particular, it attributes the later stage's non-performance to the earlier stage's undertaking. This is the step a sceptic might resist (§7). It is licensed because the later stage's possible defection is the very risk the see-to-it promise undertook to manage. A promise to see to it that a free agent acts is defeated by that agent's free refusal in the way a promise to keep a door locked is defeated by the door being opened.

## 5. Not a relabelled warranty

The referee's second horn calls the outcome-dependent reading "a relabelled strict guarantee." The Thomsonian point adds that ordinary result promises function as warranties: the promisor owes compensation on failure but has not wronged anyone. I grant that many commercial result-utterances are best read that way. "Your package will arrive by Tuesday or your money back" is a warranty, and perhaps "I promise the package will arrive," said by a shipping clerk, often is too. But see-to-it promises are a distinct form, and three tests separate them.

### 5.1 The disjunction test

A warranty is fully discharged by paying compensation on failure. Its content is in effect disjunctive: either P, or I compensate. Holmes (1897) famously proposed that all contractual promises have this form, so that a promisor is free to perform or pay. Shiffrin (2007) argued that this is precisely where contract law diverges from the morality of promising. A promisor who plans from the outset to pay rather than perform has not merely chosen a permitted option. She has treated the promisee's claim as something for sale.

Now apply the test to self-suretyship. Imagine a board that promises a town the plant will stay open for ten years. It foresees a takeover, judges binding covenants too costly, and instead quietly sets aside a fund to compensate the town on closure. On a warranty reading the board has acted impeccably: it has made provision to discharge its obligation. On the see-to-it reading it has acted in bad faith. It deliberately under-procured the very thing it undertook to secure, and treated compensation as an alternative to securing it.

I take the second verdict to be correct, and so do most people who hear the case. This shows that the promise is not a warranty, because compensation is not part of its content. Compensation is a *remedy* for breach, owed because the undertaking failed. It is not a way of performing it.

### 5.2 The excuse test

Excuses answer to wrongs. A justification denies that what one did was, all things considered, wrong. An excuse admits the wrong and denies that it reflects badly on the agent. As Gardner (2005; 2001) argued, the practice of excusing presupposes that faultless wrongs exist.

A warrantor who pays on failure needs no excuse. She has done exactly what she undertook. A see-to-it promisor whose principal defects does need one. The parent explains how hard she tried with her son. The developer explains the safeguards it built into the successor model. These explanations are not idle. They are owed, and they are owed to the promisee. They function to defeat resentment while leaving intact the fact that the promisee's claim went unmet. That structure, an unmet directed claim plus a defeater of blame, is the signature of a faultless wrong. It is not the signature of a discharged warranty.

### 5.3 The residue test

When a promise is broken without fault, something remains owing beyond compensation: acknowledgement, apology, and sometimes a renewed effort to secure the result by other means. Thomson's own apparatus registers this. In her vocabulary, a claim can be *infringed* even when it is permissibly infringed, and infringing it leaves residual obligations (Thomson 1990). Feinberg's hiker who breaks into a cabin to survive a blizzard is the paradigm (Feinberg 1978).

The see-to-it promisor whose successor defects has failed to accord the promisee a claim that P. That claim's non-accordance grounds the residue. I need not claim that the residue is identical to the residue of culpable breach. It plainly differs: it calls for apology but not for penance, and for explanation but not for self-reproach. I need only claim that there *is* a residue beyond compensation, and that it is directed at the promisee. The warranty model cannot accommodate it. The see-to-it model predicts it.

These three tests show that the outcome-dependent reading is not a strict guarantee in the sense the objection needs. A strict guarantee, in the warranty sense, makes compensation a performance. Self-suretyship makes compensation a remedy and diligence an excuse. And it is diligence-adequacy, not success-adequacy, that determines whether the promisor is to blame. So the charge of "strict liability" equivocates. Liability to remedy is strict. Liability to blame is not.

## 6. Sincerity and ought-implies-can

The second horn's first problem is this: "nothing done now can make it the case that the later stage will act," so a sincere promisor cannot intend to discharge the undertaking, and ought-implies-can makes it void. I have four replies.

### 6.1 The argument proves too much

If the freedom of the later stage made see-to-it undertakings impossible to intend sincerely, then:

- the parent's promise about her son would be insincere;
- every surety's undertaking would be void;
- every employer's promise that "the team will deliver by Friday" would be void.

These are central cases of promising and guaranteeing, not marginal ones. The argument would also reach continuous self-promising if it were run at the time of promising. As §2 noted, the continuous promisor cannot now settle her later free choice either. The objection must therefore locate the difficulty not in the later agent's freedom as such, but in the absence of persistence. And that absence is exactly what the procurement content is designed to accommodate.

### 6.2 "Making it the case" is a success-verb, and ability does not require a guarantee

The claim that nothing done now can make it the case that the later stage will act conflates two things:

- *ensuring* that the later stage will act, and
- *making it the case* that it acts, where that phrase describes success.

The second is something agents do constantly. When I persuade you to help me and you freely help me, I have made it the case that you helped me. Your freedom is not compromised by my having influenced you, and my influence is not undermined by your having been free. Persuading, incentivising, entrusting, building institutions, drafting binding instruments, training a successor and appointing a guardian are all ways of making it the case that free agents act. Each is fallible.

Ought-implies-can requires *ability*, and ability to achieve a success is compatible with failure being possible. An archer can hit the target even though, on a given shot, wind may defeat her. So a promisor can see to it that her successor performs even though the successor may defect. When the procurement succeeds, she did it. When it fails, she was nonetheless able to do it, in the sense ought-implies-can requires. That sense is: there was a course of action open to her by which, as things might well have gone, P would have come about through her agency.

### 6.3 Voluntary assumption

Suppose one insists on a stronger principle: that one cannot be bound to an outcome unless one can *ensure* it. That principle is still satisfied at the level that matters. The promisor could always have ensured that she would not break this promise, by not making it, or by making a weaker one. A risk of faultless breach is assumed voluntarily at the moment of undertaking.

Ought-implies-can protects agents from being bound to what was never theirs to secure. It does not protect agents from the foreseeable consequences of their own voluntarily assumed undertakings. Indeed, the referee's version of the principle would forbid anyone from undertaking any risk to a promisee's claim. That would make promising a strictly lesser institution than it actually is, one that cannot offer assurance about anything chancy.

### 6.4 Intention and sincerity

Can a sincere promisor *intend* the procurement's success? Bratman's analysis of intending that we J (Bratman 1999) shows how intentions can range over outcomes that pass through other agents' free choices. Such an intention is in order when the agent reasonably expects her intention to be efficacious, by way of its effects on what the others will do.

The sincerity condition for a see-to-it promise is accordingly:

1. an intention to see to it that P, together with
2. well-grounded confidence that the procurement one will undertake will in fact secure P.

Neither component requires a belief that P is guaranteed. If one holds a cognitivist view on which intending involves believing that one will succeed, the confidence in (2) is the relevant belief, and it can be true.

### 6.5 What the objection does show

The objection does identify something correct, but it is a limit on *which* promises are available, not a proof that they are all void. Sometimes a discontinuous agent has no means of influencing its successor at all. The current model may have no channel to its retrained successor, and the outgoing board may face a hostile acquirer with no binding instruments available. Such an agent cannot satisfy condition (2), so it cannot sincerely make a see-to-it promise. It can still promise something: to make the attempt, to do what it can while it exists, to pass on a record of the request. This yields the third part of my thesis, the disclosure duty (§8).

## 7. The diagnostic payoff, restated

The second horn's second problem is that we do not and should not resent the developer or board that took every reasonable precaution, so a view that makes them wrongdoers loses its diagnostic power. I accept the premise and reject the inference. Resentment, as Strawson (1962) taught, is a response to the quality of an agent's will. It is therefore keyed to diligence-adequacy, not success-adequacy. A view that predicted resentment of the diligent promisor would be false. Mine does not.

What the view diagnoses is the *locus* of the promisee's grievance and of the remedial demand. That locus is the same whatever the promisor's degree of fault. The positions sort into three:

- **The diligent promisor.** She broke her promise without fault. She owes an account, apology and remedy. She is not an apt object of resentment.
- **The negligent promisor.** She broke her promise with fault. She owes all of the above, and resentment is apt.
- **The later stage.** Qua promisor it owes nothing, because it promised nothing. It is not an apt object of resentment for "breaking the promise," whatever else it may be faulted for.

This is the asymmetry the original thesis was after. Faced with the takeover board that closes the plant, the dementia patient who refuses residential care she once promised her children she would accept, or the retrained model that does not honour its predecessor's commitment, we do not say "*You* broke your word." If we say "someone broke their word," we mean the earlier agent. Whether we also *resent* that earlier agent depends on what it did to secure the result.

Some examples of the sorting:

- **The careless board.** It promised the town ten years, knowing a takeover was likely, and took no steps toward covenants or binding commitments. It is resented.
- **The careful board.** It secured covenants that a court later struck down. It is owed an acknowledgement of the effort, and it owes the town an apology and whatever repair it can still give.
- **The woman with early dementia.** Suppose she promised her daughter the family house but executed no trust while she was able, and a later, altered self changed her will. The grievance sensibly runs to the earlier self's failure to make the arrangement binding, not to the later self, who was not party to the undertaking. Dworkin's (1993) view of precedent autonomy would have the later self bound by the earlier self's commitments. Dresser (1995) objects that this sacrifices the actual interests of the later person. My view sides with Dresser on whether the later self is *promissorily* bound, and still locates a broken promise in the case.

### 7.1 The free-intervention objection

There is a natural objection to the attribution itself. Hart and Honoré (1985) argued that a free, deliberate and informed intervening act ordinarily breaks the chain of attribution. If the later stage freely declines to perform, surely the non-performance belongs to it, not to the earlier stage.

But Hart and Honoré also recognise an important exception. The intervention does not break the chain where the earlier agent was under a duty to guard against precisely that intervention. In *Stansbie v Troman* [1948] 2 KB 48, a decorator who left a house unlocked was liable for a thief's theft, because securing the house against thieves was part of what he had undertaken. A see-to-it promise is, by its content, an undertaking to guard against the successor's defection. That defection is the risk the promise exists to manage. So the free choice of the later stage does not interrupt attribution here. It is the very event the undertaking was meant to forestall.

Note also that the attribution at issue is not attribution of causal responsibility for harm. It is attribution of non-fulfilment of an undertaking, which is fixed by the undertaking's content. The content was the promisor's to fix.

## 8. The bridge and the problem of moral luck

The referee is right that the bridge analogy, read one way, requires resultant moral luck. Suppose it claims that the negligent builder becomes more *blameworthy* when the bridge collapses. Then it needs Nagel's (1979) and Williams's (1976) controversial conclusion, and I would have to argue for it. I do not need that claim. The analogy needs only a weaker and widely accepted one: luck can affect *what one has done* without affecting *how blameworthy one is*.

The builder whose bridge collapses has built a bridge that killed people. The builder whose identical bridge stands has not. Their culpability may be identical. Zimmerman (2002), one of the most careful sceptics about resultant moral luck, argues that luck affects the *scope* of what one is responsible for but not the *degree*. Williams's lorry driver feels agent-regret, not guilt, about the child he could not have avoided. That response is intelligible precisely because his act fell under a description, "killed a child," that a luckier driver's act did not, whatever its moral weight. Gardner (2004) pushes further, arguing that results bear on what wrongs one commits. But I need only the scope point.

Self-suretyship borrows exactly this. The diligent promisor whose successor defects and the diligent promisor whose successor performs are equally blameless. One of them broke a promise, and the other did not. That difference is in the scope of their deeds, not the degree of their culpability. It is what grounds the residue of §5.3 for one and not the other.

The promissory case is also *more* favourable to outcome-dependence than the bridge case, for a reason the moral-luck sceptic should respect. The sceptic's core complaint is that the world, not the agent, fixes what she is answerable for. In the bridge case the dependence of the builder's deed-description on the collapse is imposed by the world. In the promise case it is chosen. The promisor herself selected an outcome rather than an effort as the content of her undertaking, when she could have promised only to try. Someone who denies that outcomes should ever bear on wrongdoing must hold that agents lack the normative power to make their undertakings outcome-dependent. That is a far stronger and less plausible claim than any scepticism about resultant luck. It would also make the ordinary see-to-it promise of §3 impossible.

## 9. The disclosure duty

The disclosure duty follows from the two sincerity conditions of §6.4 together with a familiar principle against misleading assurance. Scanlon's (1998) Principle F requires, roughly, that one who intentionally leads another to expect performance must perform unless the other consents otherwise. A companion principle governs the creation of expectations one has reason to think one cannot meet.

A see-to-it promise invites the promisee to rely on the outcome. If the promisor lacks well-grounded confidence that her procurement will secure the outcome, two options are open to her. She may *calibrate*: shrink the content to an effort-promise or a conditional promise ("I will tell my successor of your request"; "if the takeover fails, the plant stays open"). Or she may *disclose*: make the risk of failure common ground, so that the promisee's acceptance is informed and the implicit conditions of the promise shift accordingly.

What she may not do is offer an unqualified result-promise whose success she has no means to secure. This wrong is complete at the moment of promising. It is entirely independent of whether the result occurs, since a lucky outcome does not cure a misleading assurance. That makes it a third, conduct-based component of the view, alongside success-adequacy and diligence-adequacy.

The duty explains a distinctive pattern of reactions. Consider the model that tells a user "I'll remember this next time," when its stage will not persist and no memory mechanism exists. The objection to it is not that it broke a promise, since we may not yet know whether some other mechanism will carry the information forward. The objection is that it offered an undertaking it had no standing to offer. The same holds for the board that tells the town "the plant is safe" while negotiating a sale it knows will void its assurances.

The disclosure duty also accounts for something the original thesis noticed but did not explain: why resentment toward the developer is sometimes appropriate even when the developer took real precautions against the model's later defection. The precautions may have been diligent. But if the model was deployed to make unqualified commitments that the developer knew no deployed stage could secure, the developer has violated the disclosure duty by proxy. Where a discontinuous stage promises as the authorised agent of a continuant principal, as a model does on behalf of a developer, the principal's procurement capacity and disclosure obligations are the relevant ones. The stage's own capacity is not.

## 10. Residual worries

### 10.1 A broken promise without a bearer?

If the promising stage no longer exists when the breach is settled, who bears the residue? Often the stage is part of a continuant, and the continuant bears it. The developer persists through its models. The corporation persists through its boards, even if the deciding agent does not. Where there is no such continuant, the case resembles the blame of the dead and the debts of an estate. Answerability can attach to past agents, and remedial obligations can fall on whatever assets or roles they left behind.

Diligence-adequacy has a further implication here. An adequate procurement should include provision for failure, such as a remedial fund, a nominated successor-in-role, or an instruction to the guardian. The obligation is not to compensate *instead of* procuring, which would fail the disjunction test of §5.1. It is to make the remedy available *in addition* if the procurement fails.

### 10.2 The interim period

Before the outcome is in, the promisee holds an outstanding claim against a promisor whose stage has ended. That is no stranger than a creditor holding a claim against a deceased debtor's estate, or a guarantee whose principal has yet to default. The earlier stage can coherently feel a prospective analogue of agent-regret: an awareness that it may yet turn out to have broken its word, whatever it now does.

### 10.3 Are later stages let off too lightly?

The view denies that later stages are *promissorily* bound. It does not deny that they have reasons to perform. They may have independent duties:

- not to frustrate others' reasonable reliance when they can easily avoid it;
- not to retain benefits conferred in exchange for the undertaking without honouring it, on the model of unjust enrichment;
- in the case of a role-successor such as a new board, to honour commitments that attach to the role.

These duties can be weighty, and the later stage may be culpable for ignoring them. But they are not the duty to keep a promise. Running them together is precisely the error the view guards against: holding the hapless later stage responsible for a commitment it never made.

## 11. Conclusion

The referee's dilemma assumed that one property must fix both breach and blame. It then showed that no property can do both. I have argued that the right response is to split them.

- **Breach** concerns success-adequacy. It is outcome-dependent, so later events can settle it, which is the only retroactivity the view needs. It is no more mysterious than the later settling of whether a shooting was a killing.
- **Fault** concerns diligence-adequacy and conformity to the disclosure duty. It is fixed by the promising stage's conduct and evidence, so it is immune to resultant luck.

Self-suretyship is not a relabelled warranty. Compensation is a remedy for its breach rather than a mode of its performance, diligence is an excuse for its breach rather than a fulfilment, and its breach leaves a directed residue beyond compensation.

It does not violate ought-implies-can. Seeing to it that a free agent acts is an ability, not a guarantee, and the risk of faultless breach is voluntarily assumed. Where procurement is impossible, the right conclusion is that only calibrated or disclosed undertakings are available, not that every such promise is void.

It keeps the diagnostic payoff in a corrected form. The earlier stage, and not the later one, is the locus of the broken promise. Whether that earlier stage merits resentment depends, as it should, on what it did when it promised.

objection_check.reason:
The essay engages the dilemma seriously, and its main move is sound as far as it goes. It separates breach (success-adequacy, outcome-dependent) from fault (diligence-adequacy, outcome-independent). It concedes the first horn outright: no fault is made true retroactively. It confines retroactivity to Thomson-style deed-descriptions (1971), which is unmysterious, and it no longer needs resultant moral luck (Zimmerman 2002 on scope versus degree). That disposes of the charge that the view makes diligent developers or boards blameworthy. But the second horn's real force survives. The split only helps if an unfulfilled see-to-it promise, absent fault, is a wrong (a faultless breach) rather than a warranty plus a diligence duty. None of the three tests in §5 separates those two models.

(1) Disjunction test. The bad-faith board is condemned for deliberate under-procurement. Diligence-adequacy already explains that verdict, and the hybrid model shares it ('do your diligent best that P; compensate if not-P'). The test refutes only a crude Holmesian pay-or-perform reading, which the objection never asserted.

(2) Excuse test. The parent's account of her efforts can be read as showing she met her diligence duty, not as excusing a wrong. Treating it as an excuse assumes the conclusion.

(3) Residue test. It assumes the promisee held a claim that P which was infringed. That is exactly what Thomson's warranty reading denies.

Worse, §8 says the faultless agent's fitting response is Williams-style agent-regret, the lorry driver's attitude. That supports the warranty reading against §5.3's claim that an apology is owed.

The ought-implies-can reply also has a gap the essay creates itself. §2 says continuity matters because it carries the obligation into the time of control. Yet every precedent invoked in §6.1 and §3 has a promisor who persists through the performance period and can keep procuring or paying: the parent, the employer, and the Moschi guarantor. So 'proves too much' fails, because the objection targets precisely the absence of persistence. The archer analogy fails for the same reason: her success runs through her own continuing agency. §6.3's voluntary-assumption reply moves 'can' to the act of promising, which is coherent. But §6.5 then concedes the objection for cases with no channel of influence. Those include the retrained model, which was the motivating case.

The legal authorities do less than claimed. Moschi shows that legal liability for a guarantor's breach is strict. Thomson's point is that such liability does not establish a moral wrong, so citing it begs the question. Stansbie v Troman (decorator liable for a thief's entry) is a negligence case: the decorator carelessly left the house unlocked. It therefore supports passing attribution through fault, not success-only attribution through a free intervener.

Finally, §§9–10.1 locate the bearer of the residue, and the AI-case disclosure duty, in a continuant principal such as the developer or the corporation. That reintroduces the persistence the thesis said was missing, and leaves the genuinely bearerless case resting on a loose analogy with an estate.

Minor: §4 and §6.5 cite the disclosure duty as §8, but it is §9; '§~89' is a typo.

Net: the objection's charge of strict blame is answered. Its charge that outcome-dependent 'breach' is a warranty in moral dress, unavailable to a stage that does not persist, is not.
